stories.title: UN peacekeeping mission in Western Sahara to expire amid US, Russia vetoes
stories.summary: https://p.dw.com/p/5OtM2 Prefer DW on Google Friday's failed US draft resolution would have rebranded the peacekeeping force from MINURSO to MINUSO, dropping the 'R' which refers to referendum on the territory's self-determination. Image: FADEL SENNA/AFP Advertisement The fate of the United Nations peacekeeping mission in Western Sahara has been left in a limbo after Russia and the United States vetoed each other's draft resolutions on extending the mission that is over three decades long — just one day before the mandate expires. The peacekeeping mission, known as MINURSO, was established in 1991 to oversee a settlement plan and ceasefire between Morocco and the pro-independence Polisario Front in a territorial dispute spanning half a century. Morocco considers Western Sahara, a mineral-rich former Spanish colony, as its territory, The Polisario Front, which is supported by Algeria and represents the indigenous Sahrawi people, seeks to establish an independent state called the Sahrawi Republic. US and Russia wield vetoes On Friday, the US tabled a draft resolution at the UN Security Council (UNSC) that would have extended the mandate for one year, while making a Moroccan autonomy plan for Western Sahara the only basis for negotiations to settle the conflict, and cutting the mission's military component.

stories.title: Roy Moxham obituary
stories.summary: Roy Moxham visited India many times, partly to carry out research for his books View image in fullscreen Roy Moxham visited India many times, partly to carry out research for his books Obituary Roy Moxham obituary My uncle Roy Moxham, who has died aged 86, was a former tea plantation supervisor who in later life turned his hand to writing about tea and about India , a country he visited many times on extended trips. His most successful book was The Great Hedge of India (2001), which was published not just in English but in multiple Indian languages. The hedge of the title, which was four metres high and 2.5m wide, was made of thorny shrubs and stretched 2,500 miles across British India to form a customs line guarded by 12,000 men on behalf of the East India Company. Following independence in 1947 it all but disappeared, but Roy spent many of his visits to the country looking for vestiges, eventually finding a small surviving section. He cut a branch from it, and it is now in the possession of his brother John (my father), kept safely in his study.

stories.title: Africa: AFCON Every Two Years Again As CAF Reverses Decision
stories.summary: Africa: Afcon to Hold Every Two Years Again As CAF Reverses Decision Afcon 30 October 2026 Vanguard (Lagos) The Confederation of African Football (CAF) has reversed its decision to stage the Africa Cup of Nations (AFCON) every four years, announcing that the tournament will return to its traditional two-year cycle. The decision was unanimously approved by the CAF Executive Committee, with President Patrice Motsepe announcing the development after the organisation's Strategy Conference in Cabo Verde, held from October 7 to 9, 2026. The reversal comes after CAF reviewed its earlier plan to move AFCON to a four-year schedule and introduce an Africa Nations League as a biennial competition. CAF said the proposed Nations League would take several years to generate the financial resources and football development benefits required to make its competitions globally competitive and financially sustainable. Follow us on WhatsApp | LinkedIn for the latest headlines In a statement published on its website on Thursday, Motsepe said the decision to retain the two-year AFCON cycle was taken in the interest of African football, the confederation's 54 member associations and African players playing for clubs outside the continent. "The decision by the CAF EXCO that the CAF AFCON should take place every Two Years was based on advancing, protecting and promoting the interest of African Football and CAF's 54 Member Associations, as well as the interest of African players employed by Football Clubs outside Africa," he said.

stories.title: How Kenyans got caught in $130m US ghost student scam
stories.summary: Image source, Getty Images Image caption, US Assistant Attorney General Colin M McDonald vowed to pursue all those involved By Ondiro Oganga Reporting from Nairobi Published 30 October 2026 In May 2024, Francis Mogambi arrived in the United States after winning the Diversity Visa lottery, a programme that gives people from around the world a chance to become permanent residents. Just over two years later, the Kenyan national found himself at the centre of a US investigation into an alleged nationwide scheme to defraud the federal student aid system. On 19 October 2026, a grand jury in Nebraska indicted Mogambi on five counts of theft of government money and five counts of aggravated identity theft. Prosecutors allege that, between November 2025 and May 2026, he worked with associates in Kenya to steal the identities of US citizens and use them to fraudulently enroll fictitious students in American colleges. Once the fake students were enrolled, Mogambi allegedly diverted their financial aid payments to himself, keeping 30% and sending the remainder to his associates in Kenya.

stories.summary: Congo-Kinshasa: Global Nursing Head Flags Dangers of Misinformation After Killing of Congo Ebola Nurse Michele Sibiloni/UNICEF A nurse prepares a bed for a suspected case of Ebola in the isolation unit at Bwera Hospital, Kasese District (file photo). 30 October 2026 allAfrica.com By Peter Kenny Geneva — The International Council of Nurses (ICN) head has warned of the lethal dangers that misinformation poses to the nursing profession following the killing of a nurse in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DR Congo), who was responding to an Ebola case. ICN chief executive Howard Catton said the "tragic news" was a reminder that prevalent misinformation was particularly dangerous for healthcare staff after young men armed with machetes killed the nurse. "Health misinformation and the breakdown of trust in science is now a deadly risk for nurses and health workers," Catton posted on the media platform X on Oct. 29. The UN's Ebola coordinator and the head of the World Health Organization (WHO) on Oct. 29 deplored the killing of the nurse working to fight the disease in the DRC four days earlier. Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn In an interview with AllAfrica, Catton also warned that community health workers often supplant nurses and may be seen as an easy, cheap substitute for a skilled nursing workforce in parts of Africa. "There is both the migration of registered nurses from the continent of Africa and unemployment of nurses in Africa," said Catton. "So, as we see this growth in community health workers, we also know that registered nurses continue to leave Africa for high-income countries in Europe or North America." At the same time, many nurses on the continent remain unemployed. Catton cited UN figures showing Africa's health workforce grew to 5.72 million in 2024, up from 4.3 million in 2018, noting that such progress is not keeping pace with demand.

stories.title: Sinkholes, scarred land and scapegoats: the scourge of illegal gold mining in Johannesburg
stories.summary: Wemmer Pan Road, near Rosettenville in Johannesburg, has been occupied by illegal gold miners. Photograph: James Oatway/The Guardian There is no end in sight for the drivers of illegal mining, while police action appears ineffective By Rachel Savage in Durban Deep C ora Bailey has been encountering illegal miners ever since she first started treating injured animals in the townships around Roodepoort, west of Johannesburg, in 1991. But as the price of gold has soared, so too has activity in the abandoned mine shafts that mark the area. In late September, dozens of zama zamas – the name given to illegal miners in South Africa , meaning roughly “to take a chance” in Zulu – arrived to dig for gold across the dirt road from her charity, Claw (Community Led Animal Welfare). Soon, they were taking water for their panning and processing from the organisation’s two 25,000-litre water tanks, which are filled irregularly by the city government for the 100 or so rescued and injured animals on site. “We’ve asked them really nicely and haven’t ever refused them water to drink … But, for the first time ever, we closed the gate at 12 [midday], because we literally had about two buckets of water left,” Bailey said in mid-October.

A federal jury in Boston found that Nshimiye concealed his alleged participation in attacks against the Tutsi community while testifying in the 2019 immigration fraud trial of his former university classmate, Jean Leonard Teganya. Nshimiye fled Rwanda for Kenya in 1994 and was admitted to the U.S. as a refugee the following year. Evidence presented at his trial showed that, while a student at the University of Rwanda in Butare, he took part in attacks on the Tutsi people, including by striking them on the head with a club. Nshimiye faces up to five years in prison for each of four perjury counts and up to 10 years for obstruction of justice.

stories.title: Jeux olympiques de la jeunesse 2026: le Sénégal accueille enfin le monde du sport après 8 ans d’attente
stories.summary: Édition spéciale Jeux olympiques de la jeunesse 2026: le Sénégal accueille enfin le monde du sport après 8 ans d’attente Le 8 octobre 2018, le Sénégal était choisi pour accueillir la 4e édition des Jeux de la jeunesse (JOJ) d’été, en 2022. Un tout premier événement olympique sur le continent. La pandémie de Covid-19 étant passée par là, ces JOJ ont été reportés. Ils vont donc se dérouler à Dakar, Diamniado et Saly du 31 octobre au 13 novembre 2026. Un moment charnière pour les Sénégalais et les 2700 athlètes de moins de 18 ans attendus au pays de la Teranga.

stories.title: Ethiopia acquires Russian fighter jets and air defence systems amid war in Tigray
stories.summary: Image source, Abiy Ahmed/Facebook Image caption, The acquisition of fighter jets comes amid ongoing tensions with Eritrea By Basillioh Rukanga Â and Â Michael Teferi ,Â BBC Africa Published 29 October 2026 Ethiopia has received 12 Su-35 fighter jets from Russia, as fighting intensified in the northern Tigray region neighbouring Eritrea. Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed, who is attending the Russia-Africa summit in Moscow, described the acquisition as a "milestone" that would boost Ethiopia's defence capacity. He said Ethiopia and Russia had agreed on the deal several years ago and the warplanes had come ahead of schedule. He also said that Ethiopia had plans to acquire four S-400 air defence systems from Moscow. The Ethiopian leader said the military hardware was essential to protect the country from external threats.

stories.title: Stars and scars: the art of Atong Atem at the NGV – in pictures
stories.summary: View image in fullscreen Sahara, from the series To Be Real, 2020 Atem is celebrated for her dynamic and vibrant photographic self-portraits that explore identity, myth-making and intergenerational storytelling Share View image in fullscreen Scar 7, from the series Scars and Constellations, 2024 In her vivid self-portraits, Atem is both subject and storyteller, embodying generations of memory and tradition Share View image in fullscreen Our Neighbour Was a Witch, from the Surat series, 2022 Transforming herself through textiles, paint, costume and symbolic objects, Atem uses her body as a vessel to explore themes of race, gender and colonialism, as well as the beauty and resilience of her Dinka Bor culture and Melbourne’s African diaspora Share View image in fullscreen Men in This Town 01, from the series Men in This Town, 2024 Her practice interrogates how identity is performed, both in everyday life and before the camera, creating images in which history, memory and imagination intertwine Share View image in fullscreen The Bride Wore Pearls 1, from the series Surat, 2022 The exhibition conceptually and spatially explores ideas of movement and journeys – global themes brought to life through Atem’s personal experience of migration Share View image in fullscreen What We Are Given, 2024 Born in Ethiopia to South Sudanese parents, Atem and her family made their home in Australia in 1997 Share View image in fullscreen Celestial Cartography, from the series Scars and Constellations, 2024 Through her work, Atem links continents and generations, honouring the cultural stories and memories that have endured displacement and war Share View image in fullscreen Men in This Town 07, from the series Men in This Town, 2024 Of the exhibition, Atem said: ‘If the body is a terrain, who gets to be the geographer and who becomes the cartographer? My practice as an early career artist has sought to make signposts on the body as a politicised landscape; to document, archive and speculate. stories.title: Demands for post-poll justice as Tanzania accused of weaponising counterterrorism laws
stories.summary: Image caption, Neema Munuo, whose 18-year-old daughter Maria Chami was shot dead on the day of the election, wants the government to acknowledge her suffering By Alfred Lasteck ,Â BBC Africa ,Â Reporting from Dar es Salaam ,Â Basillioh Rukanga Â and Â Lucy Fleming Published 29 October 2026 Families affected by election-related violence in Tanzania that led to the deaths of at least 500 people a year ago have told the BBC they want justice for those killed in the protests and help with medical expenses for those injured. "We can no longer afford to pay hospital bills," Meshack Sane, who was shot in the leg, told the BBC. On the eve of the anniversary of the poll that saw President Samia Suluhu Hassan elected with 98% of the vote, rights group Amnesty International also accused her government of "weaponising counterterrorism laws to silence critics and instil fear". The opposition dismissed the result as a "mockery" of democracy as Samia's two main challengers were excluded. Tundu Lissu, the 58-year-old leader of the main opposition Chadema party, had been put on trial for treason ahead of the poll - preventing him from standing. He had been demanding electoral reforms and a verdict in his case is due next week.

stories.summary: Lina Attalah, the editor-in-chief of Mada Masr, pictured in 2017. Photograph: Roger Anis/AP View image in fullscreen Lina Attalah, the editor-in-chief of Mada Masr, pictured in 2017. Photograph: Roger Anis/AP Egypt fines prominent editor Lina Attalah and shuts independent news outlet Mada Masr Warnings of escalating clampdown on press freedom come after Cairo court convicts Attalah of managing an unlicensed website Lina Attalah, a prominent Egyptian journalist and the editor-in-chief of the news outlet Mada Masr, has been released from detention by Egypt’s authorities and had her website ordered to be shut down by a court amid an intensifying crackdown on independent media in the country. Attalah was taken briefly into custody after a Cairo court convicted her of managing an unlicensed website, prompting fresh international concerns over press freedom in Egypt. According to Mada Masr, Attalah was released after the news outlet had paid a fine of 3m Egyptian pounds ($53,500; £40,100), prompting statements of support from global human rights groups. “Lina Attalah was released after we paid the said fine,” said her lawyer Hassan al-Azhari. “In the process, we discovered that she had been sentenced in absentia in 2024 to a year in prison, as well as a fine of 20,000 Egyptian pounds,” he told AFP.

stories.summary: A map showing countries affected by active Ebola outbreaks at the headquarters of the Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention in Abuja. Photograph: Sodiq Adelakun/Reuters View image in fullscreen A map showing countries affected by active Ebola outbreaks at the headquarters of the Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention in Abuja. Photograph: Sodiq Adelakun/Reuters Africa’s ‘unprecedented’ Ebola outbreak could reach UK, says top health official Jean Kaseya, of the Africa CDC, warns of the illness spreading like Covid unless more funding is secured to increase preparedness and possible treatment The “unprecedented” spread of the Ebola outbreak means it could reach the UK and other countries, according to one of Africa’s top health officials. As the current outbreak reached 10,000 cases, with almost 5,000 deaths , Dr Jean Kaseya, director general of the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), compared the outbreak to the Covid pandemic, which first took hold in China before spreading to countries across the world, claiming millions of lives, and ravaging health systems and economies. “We want all countries to know that they are not safe if they don’t take appropriate measures,” he said. “Each country, not only in the African region, but all continents, must now increase the preparedness level and the possibility for treatment. “It is the first time three African regions have been affected [by Ebola]. The geographic extension of this outbreak is unprecedented,” he said.

stories.title: The pest I’ll never forget: the rats stood six or seven deep on the lawn beside my dormitory
stories.summary: ‘The rats began to stand their ground. They were no longer pests but now a sort of predator.’ Composite: Guardian design; Nynke van Holten; Olga Yastremska/Getty Images View image in fullscreen ‘The rats began to stand their ground. They were no longer pests but now a sort of predator.’ Composite: Guardian design; Nynke van Holten; Olga Yastremska/Getty Images The pest I’ll never forget: the rats stood six or seven deep on the lawn beside my dormitory All it took was one or two careless teenage girls giving the vermin a taste of their snacks and they became the most well-fed animals imaginable I ’ve written a fair amount about my boarding school years in Nigeria in the 90s, but never about the rats that accompanied my school experience. Picture it: thousands of girls from across the country, each bearing a suitcase or two of a term’s worth of “provisions” – cornflakes, sugar cubes, powdered milk, hot chocolate powder, and so on. All it took was one or two careless girls giving the rats a taste of the exotic and they became among the most well-fed rats in the country, enjoying a steady stream of delicious teenage-girl snacks.

Photograph: Ebrahim Hamid/AFP/Getty Images UK sanctions Sudanese military leaders implicated in El Fasher ‘campaign of rape’ Commanders suspected of sexual violence during the largest and fastest slaughter of civilians in more than 30 years have been subjected to travel ban and asset freeze Senior Sudanese commanders implicated in a “campaign of rape” have been targeted by the UK on the first anniversary of a mass atrocity that saw tens of thousands of civilians killed over several days. A year after the fall of El Fasher , the British government said it had sanctioned military leaders from both sides in the country’s ongoing conflict whom it suspected of sexual violence during the siege of the city. A total of 15 commanders from the military groups – the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) and the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) – have been subjected to a travel ban and an asset freeze .

Photograph: Patrick Ngugi/AP UK poised to miss reduced aid spending target of 0.3% of national income Calculations from the Center for Global Development say spending next year is likely to be £410m less than anticipated The UK is on course to miss its target of spending 0.3% of national income on international aid by an estimated £400m by the end of next year. Calculations from the Center for Global Development (CGD) found the UK was on course for a large shortfall in promised official development assistance at the end of 2027. The researchers said the central forecast from the Treasury’s comparison of independent experts implied UK aid would be £410m less than anticipated – at only 0.29% of national income.

stories.title: ‘We built this land’: descendants of enslaved people are reclaiming their history across South Africa’s vineyards
stories.summary: View image in fullscreen ‘We built this land’: descendants of enslaved people are reclaiming their history across South Africa’s vineyards Slavery was integral to the country’s wine industry. Now a handful of wineries are addressing its legacy and righting the wrongs of the past Groot Constantia winery, the oldest wine farm in South Africa. The building is believed to have once served as accommodation for the estate's enslaved labourers. Photograph: Tommy Trenchard/The Guardian A t Groot Constantia, the oldest wine farm in South Africa , the 450,000 visitors who pass through its gates annually can admire the picturesque vineyards sloping towards a bay ringed by mountains or enjoy a glass of sweet Grand Constance, reputed to have been Napoleon’s favourite wine. Unusually among the region’s old vineyards, there is also a museum that includes the history of slavery, run by state body Iziko Museums.

stories.title: 'I cannot teach you integrity': How employee theft is hurting small businesses in Africa
stories.summary: Image source, That Girl Boina Image caption, Kenyan food creator That Girl Boina shut her waxing studio due to employee theft By Ondiro Oganga Reporting from Nairobi Published 25 October 2026 When popular Kenyan food creator That Girl Boina took a two-week holiday to Europe, she expected to relax. A week into the trip, an Instagram direct message exposed a problem that would ultimately lead to the closure of her business. "I was at your studio, I liked everything. The only problem was that I was asked to send money to a different number. It wasn't the number on the wall," a customer wrote to her. Boina had opened Waxaholic Studio, a waxing and hydrafacial parlour in Nairobi's central business district, on 1 September 2024.
